extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators / trial counsel handling Markman hearings and claim construction
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for litigators on conducting claim construction (Markman) in district-court patent litigation, including evidence, briefing, timing, hearings, and post‑ruling strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality of claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is the first step of the two-step process for proving patent infringement; the claims of a patent legally define the right to exclude others and proper interpretation is a fundamental stage of litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction lays the groundwork for subsequent case development and controls case themes presented to the court and jury. Use claim construction to determine both infringement and validity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of intrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper claim construction requires review of the intrinsic evidence – i.e., the claims, specification, and prosecution history – and, if appropriate, extrinsic evidence. (Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis starts with the plain claim language and the specification 'is always highly relevant.' The court must ensure the claims cover what was actually invented and what the inventor intended to claim. If the inventor has acted as his own lexicographer or there is an intentional disclaimer, that dictates claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution history 'can often inform the meaning of the claim language by demonstrating how the inventor understood the invention and whether the inventor limited the invention in the course of prosecution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution history can show that the inventor narrowed claim scope. It may lack the clarity of the specification but still be informative; include relevant prosecution history in briefing to demonstrate disclaimers or limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence includes expert testimony, relevant texts and treatises, prior art patents, and both technical and non-technical dictionaries. The court may use extrinsic evidence to assist in proper construction but is not required to consider it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence may be used to understand background science or how a person of ordinary skill would interpret a term. However, the court may not rely on extrinsic evidence to vary or contradict the intrinsic evidence (Vitronics; Phillips). If extrinsic-based subsidiary facts are disputed, they require factual findings (Teva).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review standards for claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Different standards of review apply: when a district court relies only on intrinsic evidence, claim construction is reviewed de novo; when the court makes subsidiary factual findings based on extrinsic evidence, those findings are reviewed for clear error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Teva Pharms. USA, Inc. v. Sandoz, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 831 (2015) and subsequent cases. Structure your record accordingly if relying on extrinsic evidence to avoid reversible error on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning according to a person of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The court must determine the meaning the claims would have to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; claims are generally given their 'ordinary and customary meaning' as understood by that person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and support the definition of the person of ordinary skill in briefing. Declarations from technical experts are particularly useful to opine on the level of skill and how terms would be understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and scheduling strategy for Markman
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction procedures and scheduling are court- and judge-specific; a court may perform a Markman hearing at any time before charging the jury, construe claims piecemeal, or revisit earlier constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions require early Markman hearings while fact discovery is beginning (to streamline cases); others provide more flexibility. Consider pros and cons: early construction can focus issues and reduce costs or increase discovery if construction is broad; late construction allows fuller factual development but may raise costs and expert issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue/local rule considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Local patent rules vary (e.g., D. N.J., N.D. Cal., N.D. Ill., E.D. Tex., S.D.N.Y.) and may set regimented procedures, timing, term-identification requirements, and limits on claim terms and prior art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the claim construction timing and procedures of potential venues when filing or opposing transfer. Be aware some courts require identification of most significant terms and reduction of asserted claims or prior art as part of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether claim construction is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should determine if claim construction is even necessary; if claims are drafted in straightforward language, the parties may stipulate that claims have their plain and ordinary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some cases (bench trial in a patent‑savvy court) a formal construction may not be necessary. Use a stipulation or letter to the court if appropriate, but if a claim term is disputed the court must construe it for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and limitation of disputed terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the number of terms actually in dispute; courts may limit the number of terms that will be construed, forcing parties to narrow focus to potentially dispositive differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize terms that are dispositive for infringement/validity. Practical constraints include page limits and presentation time. Raising numerous or questionable terms can harm credibility; failure to narrow in good faith may lead to sanctions (see N.D. Cal. Patent L.R. 4-7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markman briefing requirements and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefing should include a background discussion of the technology, the patent-in-suit, the asserted claims, the disputed terms, relevant law on claim construction, and the definition of the ordinary person of skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each brief should expressly set forth the proposed construction for each disputed term, identify the relevant intrinsic and extrinsic evidence, apply that evidence to the proposed construction, and submit supporting evidence concurrently unless ordered otherwise. Expert declarations (similar to expert reports) are useful to introduce evidence about skill level and background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet-and-confer process before briefing
rubrics_metrics.description: Local rules or scheduling orders normally set forth a meet-and-confer process between the parties before briefing the proper construction of disputed claim terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the meet-and-confer to narrow disputed terms, discuss claim construction strategy, and identify which terms are most likely dispositive. Good-faith narrowing can preserve credibility and avoid sanction risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology tutorials and demonstratives
rubrics_metrics.description: The Markman hearing usually includes some type of technology tutorial to educate the court with respect to the background of the technology prior to construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accurate, simple, and straightforward tutorials using demonstratives, animations, or physical samples when helpful. If the court declines a pre-hearing tutorial, incorporate that background into the hearing presentation itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of live testimony and expert participation at the hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may allow testimony from qualified experts on how a person of ordinary skill would interpret claims; parties may also proffer inventor testimony, but such testimony is often given little weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider proffering experts for live testimony or having the expert attend for immediate consultation. Be cautious with inventor testimony — courts regard it as potentially self-serving and may give it little or no consideration (Bell & Howell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on letting experts argue claim scope to the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: It is error to allow experts to make arguments to the jury about claim scope when claim construction is a matter for the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the court provides jury instructions about claim meanings. Do not rely on expert argument to substitute for court's claim construction (NobelBiz; O2 Micro).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim indefiniteness as a construction argument
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may assert that there can be no construction of a disputed term because the claim is indefinite (Nautilus standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indefiniteness arguments where appropriate; consider Federal Circuit precedent on when claims are properly held indefinite as part of claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Markman strategic considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: After a Markman ruling, parties should consider tactical and procedural decisions such as seeking reconsideration, construing additional terms, checking for new precedent, amending contentions, narrowing asserted claims, dropping prior art, filing summary judgment, revisiting settlement, or stipulating to allow earlier appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific options include: motion for reconsideration of adverse term constructions; determining whether other terms become disputed; reducing asserted claims (patentee) or dropping prior art (defendant) in light of construction; amending infringement/invalidity contentions; filing summary judgment on clear issues; revisiting settlement leverage; stipulating issues for interlocutory appeal to reach the Federal Circuit sooner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving validity when construing claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A court is charged with preserving the validity of an asserted claim unless the invalidating construction is dictated by the claim and specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the only construction consistent with the claim language and written description renders the claim invalid, then the claim is invalid. Argue constructions that preserve validity where supported by intrinsic evidence (Phillips; Rhine).
